text: "Listen carefully to me, and eat what is good." In Hebrew it's "hear, hearing": shema twice. Blessing flows from listening, and listening again.
explanation:
"Why do you spend money for what is not bread?" God asks. "Listen carefully to Me, and eat what is good, and let your soul delight itself in abundance." The Hebrew repeats the verb: shamoa tishma, hear and keep hearing. It's the same pattern as "faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ."

Faith doesn't come by having heard; it comes by hearing. Last week's meal doesn't nourish you today. Keep the good news about Jesus flowing into your ears, and then into your heart. "Hear, and your soul shall live."

text: The doubled "hear, hearing" first appears with "I am the Lord who heals you." Then with family, then provision, then every blessing.
explanation:
Follow the phrase "diligently heed" (literally "hearing, hear") through Scripture. In Exodus 15 it comes with God's first revelation as Jehovah Rapha, the Lord who heals. In Deuteronomy 11 it brings "days of heaven upon the earth" for your family. In Deuteronomy 15: "You shall lend to many nations, but you shall not borrow." In Deuteronomy 28: all the blessings.

The conditions about keeping every commandment were fulfilled for you by Jesus. What's left for you is to keep listening. And notice the order: health, family, then provision. That's God's priority for you.

text: "They came to hear Him, and to be healed." Hearing came first.
explanation:
"Great multitudes came together to hear, and to be healed by Him of their infirmities." In the next chapter, the crowds from all Judea, Jerusalem, Tyre and Sidon "came to hear Him and be healed… and He healed them all." Jesus never sorted them into those who'd forgiven their enemies and those who hadn't. Whoever came, He healed.

The woman with the issue of blood came the same way: "when she heard about Jesus." If you need healing, don't just ask for prayer. Fill your ears with what God says about healing, and keep listening until faith rises.

text: "Be doers of the word, not hearers only" doesn't downgrade hearing. The doer is the one who keeps looking into the word.
explanation:
This verse is often used to imply that hearing doesn't matter much; only doing counts. But read on. The "hearer only" glances in the mirror of the word, walks away and forgets what he looks like. The doer "looks into the perfect law of liberty and continues in it." That's continual hearing.

See yourself in the word (righteous, more than a conqueror, a new creation) and keep looking. When you're full of the word, you can't help acting on it. It's a one-time hearing that fades. "This one will be blessed in what he does."

text: Israel heard the good news of the promised land, but "the word they heard" didn't profit them. The tense means they heard it once.
explanation:
"The gospel was preached to us as well as to them; but the word which they heard did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in those who heard it." They'd been told about houses they didn't build and vineyards they didn't plant, yet a generation died in the wilderness.

The verb is past tense, aorist: they heard it once and thought they knew it. Your low seasons often follow seasons of not hearing. Keep listening to the good news, even sermons you've heard before. Faith comes by hearing, not by having heard.

text: Ten people compliment you and one criticises you. Guess which one you remember?
explanation:
Ever since the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, we have a pull toward the negative. One unkind remark can outweigh a hundred kind ones. Adam and Eve had a garden full of trees and fixed their eyes on the one they couldn't have.

That's exactly why you need to keep hearing good news. Left alone, the mind drifts to worry and fear. "Whatever things are true, noble, just, pure, lovely, of good report… meditate on these things." The gospel is literally good news. Choose to feed on it, deliberately and often.

text: Can't sleep? Preach to yourself: "The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want."
explanation:
David said, "I meditate on You in the night watches." Lying awake can become a gift. When worrying thoughts keep you up, quote a psalm you know by heart, quietly and slowly: "He makes me to lie down in green pastures; He leads me beside the still waters."

You can hear the word through a preacher, but you can also be the preacher to yourself. That's what meditation means: muttering God's word under your breath. Often, after just a few times through, peace settles and sleep comes, and you wake up rested.
